scope.end: 8b: Rav Mari's question about a dog chasing her

sections.title: *Shaveh Kesef* Without a Set Value: The Priest's Own Valuation
sections.gist: Continuing the question of whether an item used as money needs a set value: the Gemara deflects Rav Yosef's *pidyon ha'ben* proof with the priest's own valuation, and Rav Ashi limits that to a great man like Rav Kahana.

bullets.text: The shiur's framing: for Rav Yosef, *shaveh kesef* stands in for money, so it must share money's defining trait, a set value. For Rabba, it is an object of value in its own right, so a credible valuation by the recipient is enough.

Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot): silk needs no *shuma* because its value is roughly known. Precious stones and pearls vary so widely that an appraisal is needed, since she cannot rely on an estimate of their worth.
Hence Tosafot: the custom is to betroth with a ring that has no stone. At the chuppah the witnesses confirm only that the ring is worth at least a perutah, so no specific value is being represented.

children.title: Calf or Cloak 'Worth Five Sela': Not Its Value but the Priest's Acceptance
children.gist: The Gemara deflects Rav Yosef's proof: the items are really worth less than five sela, and the son is redeemed only because the priest agreed to value them at that amount, as Rav Kahana did.

bullets.text: The Gemara rejects the proof. The calf or cloak is actually not worth five sela. In the second clause the son is redeemed because the priest accepted it at that value.
So it was with Rav Kahana, a priest, who took a cloth from the father of a firstborn and said: "For me, this cloth is worth five sela."

On this reading the issue is not market value or a formal *shuma*. It is whether this recipient really values the item at the required amount. That fits Rabba's view that *shaveh kesef* need not behave like money.
Tosafot raise the possibility that Rav Kahana was not a priest himself but married to a priest's daughter, implying that she too can receive the redemption.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Only a Great Man Who Needs a Head Cloth
children.gist: Rav Ashi limits the priest's own valuation to someone like Rav Kahana, and Mar bar Rav Ashi's purchase shows that such a man does pay more for a cloth.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: this works only for a priest like Rav Kahana, a great man who must wear a cloth on his head. Others, who have no such need, cannot say it is worth that much to them.
Support: Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a cloth from Rabba's mother, from Kovei, for thirteen dinars although it was worth ten, because he needed one.
Without real need, an inflated valuation counts for nothing: *batlah da'ato etzel kol adam*. For Rabba the valuation must be subjective, but credible.

sections.title: R. Elazar: 'A Hundred' Promised, One Dinar Given
sections.gist: R. Elazar reads the promised hundred as a condition and the dinar as the betrothal money. The Gemara defends him against a baraita about counting out a hundred, then explains that baraita's copper and flawed dinars.

chart.caption: The hundred-dinar cases: what was said, what happened, and the ruling
rows: The hundred is a condition (*al menat*), which takes effect now
He is counting; the last dinar is still in his hand
The whole sum is the betrothal money; or (Rav Ashi) she expects all of it
One copper coin she didn't notice (at night, or mixed in)
One worn silver dinar, spent with difficulty (Rav Pappa)

children.title: 'A Hundred' as *Al Menat*: Betrothed Now, Paying Later
children.gist: R. Elazar: she is betrothed at once with the dinar and he must pay the rest, because the promised hundred works as a condition, and a condition takes effect now.

bullets.text: R. Elazar: "Be betrothed to me with a hundred dinars," and he gave her one: she is betrothed, and he must complete the payment.
Reason: by handing over one dinar, he is like one who said "on condition that I give you a hundred." The dinar betroths now; the rest is a condition.
This follows Rav Huna in Rav's name: *kol ha'omer al menat ke'omer me'akhshav dami*. Whoever says "on condition" is as if he said "from now."
It is his act, handing over a single dinar right after naming a hundred, that shows the hundred was meant as a condition and not as the betrothal money.

children.title: The Counting Baraita: 'A Hundred' or 'This Hundred'?
children.gist: A baraita lets either side retract until the last dinar is given. The Gemara reads it as "this hundred" and argues over what its latter clause implies; Rav Ashi instead says counting is different.

children.title: Both Clauses 'This Hundred'? The Latter Clause as Explanation
children.gist: The Gemara answers that the baraita speaks of "this hundred", is challenged from the latter clause's wording, and replies that the latter clause explains the first. A supporting argument is offered and found inconclusive.

bullets.text: Challenge from a baraita (Tosefta 2:10): he said "with a hundred" and was counting it out. Either may retract, even when only the last dinar remains. So the betrothal waits for the whole hundred.
Answer: there he said "with this hundred", so the entire sum is the betrothal money.
Difficulty: the latter clause says "this hundred" explicitly, which implies that the first clause is an unspecified hundred.
The latter clause: "with this hundred", and it was one short, or one dinar was copper: not betrothed. One was a flawed dinar: betrothed, and he must exchange it.
Reply: both clauses speak of "this hundred". The latter clause explains the first: either may retract until the last dinar, in a case where he said "this hundred".
Support: if the first clause were an unspecified hundred and still no betrothal, it would go without saying for "this hundred"; the latter clause would be unneeded.
The support is inconclusive: the latter clause may have been stated to show that the first is unspecified, so that no one would limit it to "this hundred". The Gemara still keeps its reading.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Counting Out Shows She Expects the Whole Sum
children.gist: Rav Ashi needs no "this hundred": when he counts, she has the whole hundred in mind and will not settle for part, so both may retract until he finishes.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: counting is different. She has the entire hundred in mind and is not content with part of it, so either side may retract until he finishes.
So both cases can be an unspecified hundred. What he does with the money, handing over one dinar or counting out all of it, shows what was meant.

children.title: Copper Dinar vs. Flawed Dinar: Unnoticed, and Spent with Difficulty
children.gist: The copper dinar is one she didn't notice, and the flawed dinar that still betroths is one that can be spent, though with difficulty.

bullets.text: Copper dinar: if she knew, she accepted it and cannot retract. It is a case where he gave it at night, or it was mixed among the others and she didn't notice.
Flawed dinar: if it cannot be spent at all, it is just like copper. Rav Pappa: it is spent with difficulty.
A worn dinar is still currency, so she received in substance what was promised, with a duty on him to exchange the coin.

children.title: Collateral Instead of Money: Rav Nachman, R. Yitzchak, R. Ami
children.gist: Collateral given for a promised sum is neither the sum nor a gift, so it neither betroths nor buys. Another person's pledge held by a creditor is different, since a creditor acquires the pledge.

children.title: Rav Nachman: 'No Hundred Here, No Collateral Here'
children.gist: Collateral for a promised hundred does not betroth, and Rava's objection from a baraita is answered: that baraita speaks of another person's collateral.

bullets.text: Rava in Rav Nachman's name: "Be betrothed to me with a hundred," and he gave her collateral instead: she is not betrothed.
Reason: the hundred has not been given, and the collateral is only security, not a gift. He has given her nothing.
Rava objects from a baraita: if he betrothed her with collateral, she is betrothed.
Answer: there it is collateral belonging to others, held by the man who betroths her, following R. Yitzchak.
Compare Yehuda's pledge to Tamar, which only assured a gift promised for later.

children.title: R. Yitzchak: A Creditor Acquires the Pledge ('Righteousness to You')
children.gist: From Devarim 24:13, which calls returning the pledge "righteousness", R. Yitzchak derives that the creditor owns it to some extent, so he can betroth with it.

bullets.text: R. Yitzchak: "Restore the pledge... and it shall be righteousness to you" (Devarim 24:13). If the creditor did not acquire it, what righteousness is there in returning it? So a creditor acquires collateral.

Tosafot object that returning a garment for the night is kind in any case. They offer instead: the debtor's blessing would be verbal interest (*ribit devarim*) unless the creditor owns the pledge. Or: *tzedakah* means giving from one's own.
What does the woman then receive? She cannot use the debtor's pledge, and it is unclear whether she gains the right to collect the debt. The Gemara does not define her acquisition.

children.title: Rav Huna bar Avin's Sons: A Silver Piece Is Not the Price
children.gist: The same rule in a sale: a silver piece left as collateral for a maidservant is not payment, so the sellers may cancel when her price rises.

bullets.text: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant to be paid in copper perutot. Lacking the money, they left a piece of silver as collateral.
Her price rose and the sellers wanted to cancel. R. Ami: "There are no perutot here, and there is no silver piece here." There was no act of acquisition.
Tosafot: before the sale no debt existed, so what did the collateral secure, and could the sellers force completion or keep it? The question is left partly open.

children.title: Her Response to the Money: Destroying, Redirecting, Her Rock, Her Dog
children.gist: A run of baraitot on what she does with the money: destroying it, sending it to her father, his father or a stranger, and having it put on her rock or fed to her dog. Two questions are left unresolved.

bullets.text: Across these cases the Gemara is working out what counts as her acceptance: a formal act of acquisition, receiving a benefit, or some combination.

chart.caption: Her response to "Be betrothed to me with this" and the ruling
rows: It goes without saying: “I don't want it”
Throws it into the sea or fire
Not a test of his temper, though she must repay him
“Give it to my father” or “to your father”
Not a gift she passes on, even to her own father
…“on condition that he accepts it for me”
He receives it for her, even his father
She is not close to him
“So-and-so, on condition he accepts it for me”
“Place it on a rock”: not hers / hers
Only her own rock receives it for her
“Give the loaf to a dog”: not hers / hers
A benefit that betroths, or a duty he owes anyway? (Rav Mari)

children.continues: The next case follows directly: a loaf given to a poor person she supports, and then the "give, give" cases on 9a.

children.title: Thrown into the Sea or Fire: Rejection, Not a Test of His Temper
children.gist: Destroying the money is no betrothal, even though she will owe him for it. Throwing it back to him goes without saying.

bullets.text: Baraita (Tosefta 2:9): she took the hundred and threw it into the sea, into the fire, or anything that destroys: not betrothed.
The Gemara asks: does that imply that throwing it back before him is a betrothal? But that says "take it, I don't want it."
Answer, in the "it goes without saying" style (*lo mibaya*): throwing it back is obviously no betrothal.

Destroying it is the new point. Since she must repay him, one might think she took it as betrothal money and destroyed it to test whether he is short-tempered. The baraita teaches that she is still not betrothed.

children.title: Give It to Someone Else: Rejection, or Agency 'On Condition He Accepts'
children.gist: Sending the money to her father, his father or a stranger is no betrothal. Adding "on condition that he accepts it for me" makes that person her agent, and the Gemara explains why each case is needed.

children.title: My Father, Your Father: Each Stretches One Clause
children.gist: "Give it to my father" shows the reach of the first clause, and "your father" the reach of the second.

bullets.text: Baraita: "Give it to my father" or "to your father": not betrothed. With "on condition that he accepts it for me": betrothed.
"My father" shows how far the first clause goes. Even her own father, whom she surely wants to benefit, receiving it does not make her betrothed.
"Your father" shows how far the second clause goes. With the condition, even his father can receive it for her.
The condition turns the recipient into her *shaliach*, and his receipt is hers.

children.title: So-and-So: Why the Stranger Case Is Also Needed
children.gist: The same two rulings for a stranger. Each case alone could have been misread in the opposite direction, so both are taught.

bullets.text: Baraita: "Give it to so-and-so": not betrothed. "On condition that he accepts it for me": betrothed.
From relatives alone, one might think the condition works only because she relies on them to hold the money for her, and not with a stranger.

From the stranger alone, one might think "give it to him" fails only because she isn't close to him. With her father or his, she might be passing on as a gift money she had accepted, and so be betrothed.
Rashi: this is not like "give a hundred to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to you". There she started the arrangement herself; here she is mocking him.

chart.caption: Why the baraita teaches both the relatives and the stranger
rows: The condition works only with relatives she relies on to hold it for her
So-and-so: the condition works even with a stranger
Without the condition, a father might receive it as her gift after accepting
Father: without the condition, still no betrothal

children.title: Her Rock, Her Dog: Acceptance Through What Is Hers
children.gist: Money put on her own rock, or bread given to her own dog, betroths her. A shared rock and a dog attacking her are left *teiku*.

children.title: Place It on a Rock: Hers, Not Hers, or Shared? Teiku
children.gist: Her own rock betroths her and another's does not. Rav Beivai's question about a rock they own together is left unresolved.

bullets.text: Baraita: "Place them on a rock": not betrothed. If the rock was hers: betrothed.
Rav Beivai asks: what if the rock belongs to both of them? *Teiku*.
Rashi: her own rock acquires the money for her through *kinyan chatzer*.

Tosafot: if it were *kinyan chatzer*, a shared rock would be simple, since partners' shared property does not acquire for one of them. The issue is whether she is confident she can retrieve the money: yes on her rock, no on another's, unclear on a shared one.

children.title: Give the Loaf to a Dog: Only Her Own
children.gist: A loaf given to her own dog betroths her; to someone else's dog, it does not.

bullets.text: Baraita: "Be betrothed to me with this loaf," and she said "give it to a dog": not betrothed. If the dog was hers: betrothed.
It is left open whether she acquires the loaf through her dog, as with her rock, or whether the betrothal money is the benefit of having her dog fed at his expense.

children.title: Rav Mari: A Dog Chasing Her: Rescue as Benefit? Teiku
children.gist: If the dog was attacking her, does being rescued count as a benefit that betroths her, or can she say he was obliged to save her anyway? Left unresolved.

bullets.text: Rav Mari asks: a dog was chasing her to bite her, and she said "give the loaf to the dog." What is the law?
Perhaps she commits herself through the benefit of being rescued from the dog.
Or she can say: you were obligated to rescue me anyway, under "Neither shall you stand idly by the blood of your neighbor" (Vayikra 19:16), so she owes him nothing.
*Teiku*: the question stands.

key_terms.sense: an item worth money used in place of money
key_terms.definition: Property that is not currency but has monetary value, which can serve in place of money in transactions that require money, such as betrothal by money.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether *shaveh kesef* must have a set value like money (Rav Yosef) or only a real, even subjective, value (Rabba), as seen in the priest's own valuation.

key_terms.definition: A formal assessment of an item's worth, needed where the parties' agreement depends on knowing its value.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The shiur ties Rabbeinu Tam's distinction between silk and gemstones, and the custom of a plain ring, to whether an item given for betrothal needs appraisal.

key_terms.definition: A father's obligation to redeem his firstborn son by giving a priest five sela, in coin or in property of that value.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A calf or cloak "worth five sela" redeems the son because the priest accepted it at that value, as Rav Kahana did with a cloth; Rav Ashi limits this to a great man.

key_terms.sense: a condition attached to a transaction
key_terms.definition: A stipulation introduced by "on condition that", under which the transaction takes effect now, provided the condition is later fulfilled.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Elazar treats "with a hundred" plus one dinar given as "on condition that I give you a hundred", so she is betrothed at once, following Rav Huna in Rav's name.
aliases: kol ha'omer al menat ke'omer me'akhshav dami

key_terms.sense: collateral for a debt or payment
key_terms.definition: An object pledged as security for a debt or promised payment, held by the creditor until it is paid.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Collateral for a promised sum neither betroths nor buys, but a creditor acquires another's pledge enough to betroth with it (R. Yitzchak).

key_terms.sense: an agent receiving on another's behalf
key_terms.definition: A person appointed to act for another, whose act, such as receiving money, counts legally as that person's own.
key_terms.on_this_daf: "On condition that he accepts it for me" makes her father, his father or even a stranger her agent, so the money betroths her.

key_terms.definition: The principle that a person's property, such as a courtyard, can acquire objects placed in it on the owner's behalf.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rashi explains that money placed on her own rock betroths her through *kinyan chatzer*; Tosafot reject this because of the shared-rock question.

judgment_calls: The opening lines (8a.10–11) close the silk/*shaveh kesef* debate that began on 7b; grouped them under one parent (s1) with the Gemara's deflection and Rav Ashi's limit as children, rather than two top-level sections.
Tosafot/Rabbeinu Tam on silk vs. gemstones and the plain-ring custom have no anchor in these lines; placed them as shiur bullets in s1's parent bullets rather than inventing a section.
Rav Ashi's answer (8a.20) could be a sibling of the whole counting-baraita discussion; kept it as the second child of s6, since it answers the same challenge from the baraita.
The copper and flawed dinars (8a.21–22) analyze the latter clause quoted in s7; kept them as a separate child of s4, where they fall, not nested in s7.

Father/his father and so-and-so grouped under one parent (s16), since the Gemara treats the stranger case as a necessary pair to the father case; rock and dog grouped (s19) as acceptance through her own property.
Rav Mari's question made a flagged child of the dog section, although it shares line 8b.12 with the dog baraita.
coverage_notes: 8a.1–8a.9 (the end of Rav Yosef's set-value principle, the Hebrew slave baraita, Rabba's symbolic-exchange reading, and Rav Yosef's statement of the *pidyon ha'ben* proof) fall before this outline's first line; the essay's treatment of them is left out.
The essay attributes the head-cloth limitation to Mar bar Rav Ashi; the text has Rav Ashi say it, with Mar bar Rav Ashi's purchase of a cloth brought as support. Followed the text.

The essay says the Gemara concludes "silk does not require appraisal"; that ruling does not appear in the lines provided. Tosafot's discussion is kept as shiur analysis only, with no Gemara bullet for the ruling.
The essay says Rabba answers the *pidyon ha'ben* proof; the text presents it as the Gemara's rejection. Followed the text, keeping Rabba's view as shiur framing.

The essay's account of the counting baraita (both clauses an unspecified hundred; a defective coin replaceable in the first clause) does not match the text. Followed the text's order: "this hundred"; the difficulty from the latter clause; both clauses "this hundred"; the support and its rejection; Rav Ashi's "counting is different".
The essay calls the questioner on the rock "Rav Bibi"; the text has Rav Beivai. Followed the text.
The essay describes the maidservant purchase as with cash and a single seller; the text has copper perutot and sellers (plural). Followed the text.
The essay reads "give it to my father" as mocking; the text says her father is one she wants to benefit. Followed the text; Rashi's "she is mocking him" is kept as shiur on the so-and-so case.
Rav Mari's question about a dog chasing her (8b.12–13) is not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the text and flagged.
The loaf given to a poor person (8b.14) and the story that follows fall after the last line; left for the next outline.
